articles.text: Theater building over budget; additional funding needed To complete construction of the new high school theater building, Piedmont School District has borrowed $1.8 million at no interest from the Piedmont Education Foundation to cover necessary costs. A $66 million bond (H1) was approved in 2016 to pay for a new classroom building ($30 million) and companion theater building ($20 million). The classroom (STEAM) building was scheduled to be completed by August 2020, but was delayed in part because of COVID. The theater building, currently in progress, was scheduled to be open by August this year, but is not expected to be completed until late this year. Both projects went over budget, requiring “value engineering.” The $66 million bond included a $4.8 million contingency. articles.text: In her letter to the editor in last week’s Post, Hannah Pinkham condemns the police as instruments of “fear, oppression, and destruction.” I remember experiencing a sense of “fear, oppression, and destruction” on September 11, 2001, when the Twin Towers came down. I also remember that 70 police officers lost their lives that day because when disaster struck, and thousands of civilians did whatever they could to escape the danger, the police did what they were trained to do: They ran toward the danger. That is the job these men and women enlist to do. They put on their uniforms and risk their lives each day to shield the rest of us from danger. Ms. Pinkham’s letter parrots many of the woke theories about the police that have been marinating in our academic centers for years. They are based on exaggerations, distortions, and outright falsehoods. Unfortunately, they gained a significant degree of traction outside academe with the brutal killing of George Floyd. If evidence is needed of the consequences of accepting these theories, consider what has happened since Mr. Floyd’s death, with the advent of the “Defund the Police” campaign. Short on resources and subject to scorn and 20/20 hindsight scrutiny, the police – those so-called instruments of oppression – scaled back their presence. And what happened to all those people Ms. Pinkham identifies as the victims of their “oppression?” They became the victims of the greatest crime spike [in the U.S.] in recent history. Throughout our country, attacks on the police have led to a dramatic rise in homicides. There has been a 36% rise in homicides in Bay Area cities during the first six months of 2021. In Chicago, a city run by people who accept the same woke dogmas promulgated by Ms. Pinkham, there were 104 shootings over the Fourth of July weekend alone. Among the victims were 13 children, some as young as five years old. So far this year, Chicago has seen more than 2,020 shootings, a 58% increase over the year 2019, before the “Defund the Police” campaign took root. articles.text: The task of overcoming poverty in the East Bay is shared by everyone who lives here. All of us want to live in neighborhoods that are stable, secure and thriving. One non-profit has been working for 15 years on this problem by focusing on job-training programs for low-income workers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. The Strive for Change Foundation, a (501c3) non-profit, believes all workers deserve the chance to improve their job skills and get better jobs. Increased income helps low-income workers achieve a more stable and financially self-sustaining future. Their families, their neighborhoods, and everyone around them benefits. The Strive for Change Foundation was founded in 2006 by Piedmont resident Lester Ellis and a small group of individuals who wanted to support workforce development programs for low-income workers. They decided to gather their donations into a single fund and use it to give grants to multiple non-profit job-training programs throughout the East Bay. Since that time, the Strive for Change Foundation has donated more than one million dollars to dozens of job-training programs in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Grants range in size from about $5,000 to a high of $12,500. Strive for Change supports organizations who help low-income workers with barriers to employment develop the skills they need to find better jobs, keep those jobs, and build stable futures for their families. Strive for Change operates on three core principles. First, unlike larger foundations that serve international endeavors, Strive for Change focuses exclusively on the working poor in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Second, 100% of donor contributions go to the agencies identified as worthy of support. The all-volunteer Board covers all administrative costs such as mailing, postage, and informational materials. And third, Strive for Change rigorously vets the agencies that seek support. The Board meets annually with the Executive Directors and program managers, and asks them the hard questions about budgets, graduation rate, job placement and retention rates. This process helps Strive supporters to be better-informed donors as well. Strive’s Board of Directors meets monthly to review grantee programs and discuss ongoing concerns, among them fundraising and Board development. Most Board members spend an average of two to five hours per month on Board activities. Board positions are available in the areas of workforce development, fundraising, writing and graphic design. For many members of the East Bay community, every hour is a struggle to put food on the table and keep a roof overhead. Minimum wage earners often require three full-time jobs just to provide their family with basic necessities. Post-Covid, many of those underpaid jobs will no longer exist. The need is greater than ever before for job-training programs that demonstrably help hardworking, ambitious people get better jobs. More information about the Strive for Change Foundation can be found at www. striveforchangefoundation.org. For more information contact Board President Miriam Mangini at miriamvmangini@gmail.com. –Langston Hughes 1901-1967 U.S. novelist, playwright, poet, social activitst

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council has decided to delay the decision to designate four parking spaces on Bonita Avenue by the Rec. tennis courts as Electric Vehicle (EV) charging stations. The consideration was on the agenda for the July 19 meeting. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit told councilmembers that staff had requested to pull the agenda item, and return to city council for more discussion in August. “Progress is being made with East Bay Community Energy in addressing the concerns that council expressed in the past. Our preference is to bring a fully-baked plan that we feel is going as far as we can go with East Bay Energy, but it’s just not ready yet,” Benoit said. A decision was initially delayed on the June 21 meeting. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) and city staff worked together to plan the installation of EV charging stations, serving four existing, angled public parking spots next to the tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. The proposed 10-year agreement would allow EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. The stations would be maintained and operated by EBCE, at no cost to the city. CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo called the proposal a “winwin” for the city in terms of reaching its ambitious Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse emissions. According to data collected from a survey conducted by FM3 Research in June 2020, 26% of Piedmonters own an electric vehicle. The survey asked respondents, “as part of the Climate Action Plan, the City is considering expanding access to electric vehicle chargers in Piedmont. The City would partner with East Bay Community Energy to install publicly accessible chargers on streetlights in three key locations in Piedmont, and to install publicly accessible high-speed charging ports in four spaces in Community Hall Parking Lot. East Bay Community Energy will pay the full cost to install chargers and will own and maintain them. Each charger would be adjacent to a designated electric vehicle-only parking spot. Does this program generally sound like something you would support or oppose?” A total of 79% of respondents supported the program, with 49% listing as “strongly supporting” and 16% opposed the program. On a statewide level, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to set a target that 100% of in-state sales of new passenger vehicles will be zero-emission by 2035. The order was signed in September 2020, following a catastrophic wildfire season.

articles.text: Fentons Creamery is considered an Oakland landmark, serving ice cream in the East Bay for over 100 years. The ice cream parlor familiar to Piedmonters opened in 1894 on the corner of 41st and Howe streets before moving a few blocks away to its present location on Piedmont Avenue in 1961. Years earlier, in 1894, Eldridge Seth’s grandson, Melvin Fenton, was responsible for inventing Rocky Road ice cream, arguably its most famous creation. Fentons candymaker George Farren made a Rocky Road candy bar and decided to blend it into an ice cream flavor in the late 1920s. Other Fentons original ice creams are Swiss Milk Chocolate and Toasted Almond. In 2001 an arson fire destroyed part of the building, but the cost to fully restore the parlor was more than $2 million. The renovated creamery included a new grill, a larger dining room and more items on the menu. Eight years after the rebuilding, Pixar featured it in its Oscar Award-winning film, Up. It seems that director Pete Docter, producer Jonas Rivera, and other Pixar employees were regular customers. In 2007 Fentons opened a second location in Vacaville at the site of the former Nut Tree restaurant and later a small ice cream shop in the Oakland International Airport. and strawberry. Asked about the Piedmont connection, Rodgers said, “Fentons is very well known for giving back to the community and a lot of community outreach.” He went on to say that there is no robust advertising needed, because people fill the parlor largely through word-of-mouth. “The love that we put into the ice cream really shows to our customers,” Rodgers added, noting that customers come from throughout the Bay Area. The stability of Fentons has been one of its strengths. Customers who have been visiting the Piedmont Avenue parlor enjoy seeing familiar faces among the staff. Many of the employees have been working there for over 20 years. articles.text: Piedmont police to visit with neighbors ta block parties The Piedmont Police and Piedmont Fire Departments hereby invite all community members to celebrate the 2021 National Night Out next Tuesday August 3. As part of National Night Out, members of the Piedmont Police and Fire Departments will visit registered neighborhood events ranging from small potlucks and BBQs to community meetings and block parties throughout the city. “We hope neighbors near and far will join us for a fun and informative evening. There will be delicious Mexican food for purchase from Abel’s Taco Truck, music, games and friendship. After a 16-month pandemic we all feel a little more isolated from one another, so please join us and help continue to build a more caring place to live,” said host Marilyn Weber. As residents and police officers come together, the main objective continues to be one of the most effective crime prevention techniques of all – getting to know your neighbors. The event sends a message to criminals that neighborhoods are organized and united in preventing crime. “We are excited by this year’s National Night Out event as our community comes together once again to connect and affirm the importance of community safety.” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “So much has changed since our last event two years ago. We know the myriad of challenges that face us as a collective. As a police department, we know our connection with the community is essential to achieving our highest standards in service. National Night Out offers us an opportunity to connect and come together.” To register your own BBQ block party event, obtain flyers for your event, and gain more information, contact Officer Nicole Casalnuovo at ncasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov. Both time slots offer daily activities, such as staff-led outside games, art projects, cooking lessons, team-building activities, and free play, all designed for children at different age levels. While on hiatus due to the coronavirus pandemic, and subsequent school district closure, the program was re-imagined last year as the virtual program “Camp Smart Start” and department-organized play pods. Schoolmates returns this year as a license-exempt program. It has been required to operate as a licensed childcare facility under California law, because it operated as a full-day program, open from 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. “As a licensed childcare facility, Schoolmates had to adhere to state-mandated requirements, which proved challenging,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns told Recreation Commissioners at a July 21 meeting. The state required all staff members to pass a background check and meet strict education requirements, which includes completed units in early childcare education. Child to staff ratio could not exceed 14 to one. Stearns explained that department staff will still do background checks and adhere to all recommended child-to-staff ratios, which he said is often well under the state requirements and are “typically at a 1 to 10 [staffto-child] ratio.” “We are excited about this change, because it means we’ll be able to serve more families and continue to bring in great staff, knowing that we are following the rules as they should be,” Stearns said. “And we’re excited to move away from computer screens and to get back into what we’ve been known for all these years, which is high-quality, play-based childcare.” Drop-in registration caused Schoolmates to routinely exceed licensing capacity, and “put staff in a difficult position of either turning children away, or being out of compliance,” Stearns said. The license-exempt status allows the program to expand its capacity limits – 44 at Beach, 50 at Havens, and 40 at Wildwood – to a more flexible capacity in line with Fire Marshal Room capacity limits. Allowed capacity nearly doubles at Beach and Wildwood locations, from 44 to 77 and 40 to 72, respectively, when the program becomes license-exempt. Stearns said that these changes will not in any way affect the well-being, or educational aspects of the program. “We intend to follow every rule for licensing. [There are] clearly defined guidelines, staff training, and classroom setup that we will continue to do, with the exception of the room capacity, essentially,” he said, adding that staff would not be negatively affected by the change, either. Registration opens today, July 28 for the after-school care program and is accessible via Community Pass online. Residents with questions may contact Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns at jstearns@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Kimberly Bonacum has retired from her position as an Occupational Therapist with Piedmont School District for 18 years. She worked at every school site as a paraeducator and occupational therapist, helping students from preschool to 12th grade overcome challenges and gain confidence. “Kim was always kid-centered and came up with creative and inventive ways to reach her students. She is a true gem, and we will miss having her as part of our special education team,” said Carrie Poole, School District Special Education Program Coordinator. The work of an OT is centered on fine motor, visual perception, and sensory motor skills. Bonacum took an inventive approach to her work, creating physical tools and starting the “Food School” for preschoolers. Bonacum’s professional journey began at Yale hospital in New Haven, Connecticut, working in adult rehabilitation. She took the opportunity to work with the hospital in developing a Newborn Intensive Care Unit program for therapists. After working with adults and then with newborns, Bonacum moved to California and began her career working with children. In 2003 she worked as a oneon-one paraeducator at Havens but had her sights set on leading the Occupational Therapy Program for General Education. One year later the position opened up and Bonacum began working with students in grades K-2. “When students succeed, they feel more confident, whether it is with their ability to write legibly or effortlessly. OT is also just about helping a student overcome,” Bonacum said. Bonacum may be best known for starting the “Food School,” getting kids in preschool to explore new foods. “We worked on sensitivity, which we call sensory defensiveness,” Bonacum explained. “As the student explores foods, whether it is touching it smelling it, playing with it actually, it is not so scary.” Bonacum expanded the teaching to parents by giving them chocolate covered crickets – real crickets. “I handed the crickets to the parents so each of them could experience holding a food they had never had before. We talked about what they felt while just holding it. It is no different from when a kid gets broccoli; it is something new,” she said. Bonacum recalled a moment of affirmation that the Food School was working. “I had a parent call me to say, ‘my son just ate a piece of salmon,’ and she was just in tears. As a parent if you can’t get your child to eat, you are always Kim Bonacum worked as an Occupational Therapist at all schools in Piedmont School District. worried about nutrition. It can be something that overwhelms you.” The General Education Program Bonacum led was eliminated by the school district in 2009, and so Bonacum adapted to being a one-on-one paraeducator while also working part-time as at an OT at Children’s Hospital in Oakland. In 2013 Bonacum returned to full time work at all five Piedmont schools, working with students of all ages who needed support. Bonacum witnessed a change in attitude towards occupational therapy during her career with the acceptance and adaptation of OT methods by teachers. “Teachers have now become much more onboard with what we call ‘sensory strategies’ in the classroom. They really saw how some of these strategies or tools were helpful for learning, so they became the ones seeking me out. That openness was exciting to see.” The greatest challenge in her career was likely the shift to distance learning in 2020 due to COVID. “Never in a million years did I think I would do OT over a computer for a job. But we made it work.” she said. Bonacum has moved to Maine with her husband Doug, and after taking a break will pursue her business, Mindful Fidgets, selling fine motor and sensory tools for kids. First, though, she and her husband are planning to walk the historic 500-mile Camino de Santiago pilgrimage in Spain, walking from village to village. articles.text: One of the four new courses offered at Piedmont High School this fall is Guitar Engineering, to be taught by veteran Physics instructor Marna Chamberlain, who came up with the idea for the class. Students will construct their own solid-body electric guitar. The course will cover the different types of wood used in guitars, guitar headstock design features, and math application in a guitar. Physical science aspects of the guitar will be explored in addition to mechanical systems, concepts of sound, string tension, fretboard layout, intonation and electronic circuitry. Students will begin the year by learning to use the tools in the new Fabrication Maker’s Lab while building a simple instrument from a cigar box. The bulk of the course will be creating full-size guitars. After fine tuning their finished instruments, students will have the opportunity to use the new CNC and 3D printers to manufacture additional projects. Guitar Engineering will be offered for the first time at Piedmont High this fall, 21 students so far have signed up for the year-long course. Science, technology, engineering and mathematics concepts that relate directly to guitars will be used to help students make an applied learning connection. “I feel that there needs to be classes available for kids to explore and build things for the pure enjoyment and experience,” explained Chamberlain. “Guitar Engineering integrates multiple subjects together. A cross-curricular course is important for students to see the interconnected of multiple disciplines which go beyond a single subject matter,” said School Board President Cory Smegal. To learn more see: Guitarbuilding.org.

articles.text: Chabot Space and Science Center in the hills above Oakland opened its doors for the first time in over a year to hold a press conference on Tuesday July 20 announcing a new exhibit space in partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center. Chabot’s Executive Director Adam Tobin and the Director of Ames, Eugene Tu, provided details of the new partnership before Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer volunteers displayed prototypes of the new exhibits that will be in The Nasa Experience exhibit. The NASA Experience aims to put the visitor into the role of a NASA researcher. Hands-on STEM studios will actively teach principals such as aerodynamics through wind tunnels, spectroscopy and how to make a comet from scratch. The exhibit will highlight the process of getting into space through interactive challenges, models, and artifacts. At the conference, Galaxy Explorer volunteers, including Piedmont students Helena Lowe and Sage Mosley, led activities and demonstrations for the media audience. Lowe ran the interactive spectroscopy demonstration which reveals the dispersion of an object’s light into its component colors when viewed through special glasses. “We have refraction gradings here which basically separate the different wavelengths of lights. Our demo shows spectroscopy, which scientists use to determine what stars and atmospheres are composed of. This was used to determine the existence of dark matter, because things were traveling too fast for the mass we saw,” Lowe explained. Mosley, a PHS junior, has volunteered as a Galaxy Explorer at Chabot for 18 months and became the youngest paid intern at the Center this summer. She ran the rocketry demonstration at the press conference, displaying components of the rockets she and her team created. Mosley has high hopes for the new exhibit and the new partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center. “I think it’s a really good expe- 2021 PHS graduate and Chabot Galaxy Explorer Helena Lowe gives a demonstration showing the visible light spectrum [photo taken through refraction glasses]. Galaxy Explorers led members of the media into Chabot through the atrium for the first time in 16 months. rience for young teens and kids to get involved with more hands-on activities with NASA, and aerospace engineering,” she said. The exhibit will be located downstairs by the cafe and will open in November this year when the Center reopens to the public after a 20-month closure. The partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center extends into the larger community. This five-year agreement between Chabot and Ames pools resources to expand on Chabot’s existing involvement in Oakland schools through their “Learning Everywhere” initiative. Director of Oakland’s School Board Gary Yee also spoke at the press conference, lauding this new expansion of space science into Oakland’s classrooms. The partnership also creates tangible STEAM career pathways by developing explicit connections between NASA’s career opportunities and Chabot’s youth development programs. NASA will provide speakers, field trips, and independent study on the missions and technology associated with work happening in Mountain View at NASA Ames in collaboration with Chabot’s Galaxy Explorers program. Eugene Tu, Director of NASA’s Ames Research Center (left), and Chabot Executive Director Adam Tobin unveil an Astrobee robot that is being developed as a free-flying research robot on the International Space Station.

articles.text: The University of California (UC) system made the most admission offers to California residents applying as freshman or transfers in its history. The record-breaking year saw more than 200,000 applicants vying for 46,000 freshman seats. Systemwide freshman admissions jumped 11 percent in 2020, the UC Office of the President announced in a statement on July 19. Admission of California freshmen reached an all-time high this year with 84,223 students, an increase of 5% over 79,953 from 2020. “These remarkable numbers are a testament to the hard work and resiliency of students and their families across California,” said UC President Michael Drake. “I am particularly heartened by the social and economic diversity of those offered a place at UC. Fall will be an exciting time on our campuses.” “As the data make clear, UC is continuing to honor its commitment to guarantee admission to high-performing California high school students and providing a clear pathway for talented community college students to join us,” said Han Mi Yoon-Wu, executive director of Undergraduate Admissions at UC. Applications to schools within the UC system were vastly different this year due to the closure of schools in the state for months as a result of the COVID pandemic. pages.text: Wednesday, July 28, 2021 9 UC offers record-high admissions to Calif. students By Allyson Aleksey The University of California (UC) system made the most admission offers to California residents applying as freshman or transfers in its history. The record-breaking year saw more than 200,000 applicants vying for 46,000 freshman seats. Systemwide freshman admissions jumped 11 percent in 2020, the UC Office of the President announced in a statement on July 19. Admission of California freshmen reached an all-time high this year with 84,223 students, an increase of 5% over 79,953 from 2020. “These remarkable numbers are a testament to the hard work and resiliency of students and their families across California,” said UC President Michael Drake. “I am particularly heartened by the social and economic diversity of those offered a place at UC. Fall will be an exciting time on our campuses.” “As the data make clear, UC is continuing to honor its commitment to guarantee admission to high-performing California high school students and providing a clear pathway for talented community college students to join us,” said Han Mi Yoon-Wu, executive director of Undergraduate Admissions at UC. Schools in the UC system suspended the letter-grade requirement for high school classes in 2020, and the full 2020-21 academic year. articles.text: Smokey conditions around Lake Tahoe basin The Tamarack Fire wages in Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest and has consumed 67,764 acres, with 45 percent containment as of Monday, July 26. The blaze began on July 4 and was one of several fires sparked by lightning in the area. It expanded by wind the following week. The fire is burning just 25 miles south of South Lake Tahoe As of yesterday, July 27, the blaze was 59 percent contained and air quality had improved. For those considering traveling to Lake Tahoe, the National Weather Service issued a statement that smoke will continue to impact the region. While conditions may incrementally improve during the daytime hours, poor air quality is expected for the foreseeable future. “There will be periods late in the day where air quality could improve somewhat around RenoTahoe and the Eastern Sierra,” wrote the National Weather Service in Reno. “However, for the most part you should expect poor air quality to persist, especially at night and in the mornings.” The National Weather Service also issued a flash flood warning for Lake Tahoe, Douglas County, and Western Nevada on Monday, July 26 due to weather patterns spreading north into east central Photos courtesy of TahoeSouth.com A webcam photo of Timber Cove in South Lake Tahoe, showing the air quality and visitors still swimming on Monday, July 26. Slow moving hybrid type thunderstorms could produce short periods of heavy rains in the area. which could impact loose debris created by the fire. As of Monday, the South Lake Tahoe had a U.S. Air Quality Index rating of 121 in the “Unhealthy for sensitive groups” range. However, that number dipped back into the green healthy range for both South and North Lake Tahoe on Tuesday night after rain showers in the area.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek A “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” will be held on August 12 at the Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek, featuring the works of over 20 renowned Northern California artists. Each year, the garden hosts an annual art show and sale that showcases sculptural art against the natural backdrop of the location. Live jazz music will be performed, and beer and wine is available for purchase. A special members-only after-hours evening sculpture stroll begins at 5 p.m. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The garden is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Tuesday through Thursday, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday. For a full list of items in bloom see the website: https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/wp/ wp-content/uploads/Whats-InBloom-July-2021.pdf. For more information, see: https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/.

articles.text: Country and Western music composer Hank Wiliams. Certain items go well together: ham and eggs, hotdogs and mustard, beer and pretzels, country music and barbecue. Let’s begin with the music. When we think of great songwriters, Schubert usually comes first. Who else is in the running? The Beatles for sure. But I include Hank Williams in the short list of great song composers. Hank Williams’ songs always speak to the human condition. They have universality and a timeless quality. Every song is a complete story. Some songs like “Ramblin Man” will send chills up and down your spine. Others, like “Move it on Over” are a humorous look at a guy who is having marital problems. Williams could have been writing about the great English baroque composer Henry Purcell when he wrote that song. As history tells it, Purcell returned home late one night from the pub. His wife, obviously very angry with him, locked him out of the house. It was a cold night. Purcell got pneumonia and died. As for Williams, he suffered a lifetime of personal and physical problems. The great country singer-composer, Roy Acuff warned him, “You’ve got a million-dollar talent, but a ten-cent brain.” He died at age 29 from alcohol and drugs. A sad end for a great talent. Leave it to posterity to remember the first part of Acuff’s words of wisdom – a million-dollar talent. And now to the second part of the perfect pairing – Good barbecue. After teaching my 31/2-yearoldd grandson about Schubert and Williams, I was in the mood for barbecue. A neighbor recommended Smokin Woods BBQ in the Temescal area. It is surrounded by Korean restaurants. We found a parking space and saw a long line in front of Smokin Woods BBQ. Most of the people were there for takeout. Everyone was very friendly, and they gave me good recommendations on what to order. We ordered the three-meat combo and told the hostess that we wanted to eat inside. The wait was rather long, but it gave us a chance to watch the efficiency of the two-man kitchen. Our food arrived on a large tray – attractively displayed. The pork spareribs were succulent and tender. They had a perfect natural wood smoked flavor. A beef rib was of biblical proportions – tender and moist with a crust which sealed in the flavors. The third item was barbecue chicken. We enjoyed classic collard greens flavored with smoked pork. The people at neighboring tables were enjoying many of the side dishes, including mac and cheese, a favorite of many customers. Everyone seemed to be having a good time and the atmosphere was very friendly. Smokin Woods BBQ is not for the faint at heart. It is not situated in the greatest area and is also very noisy. There are eight giant TV screens showing a variety of sports in addition to loud ambient music. I would go there again, but I might bring earplugs.

He is also the visionary behind the San Francisco performance company Cultural Odyssey, and the founder and artistic director of the world music ensemble Idris Ackamoor and The Pyramids. He is a protege of legendary Chicago clarinetist Clifford King, who learned from New Orleans jazz greats Jelly Roll Morton and Freddie Keppard. Ackamoor is a pioneer in a musical genre coined “Afrofuturism,” which explores the developing intersection of African diaspora culture with technology. For over two decades, Yerba Buena Gardens Festival has presented free outdoor music, circus, dance, poetry, theatre, and youth programs by artists from the Bay Area and around the world. The festival was cancelled last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Yerba Buena Gardens are located on Mission Street between 3rd and 4th streets in San Francisco. No sign-up is required to attend. Visit www.ybgfestival. org for a full schedule.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, July 28, 2021 Piedmont Scouts sail the seas 15 Scouts from 3 troops spend week sailing in the Caribbean By Arun Brahma On July 6th, 15 Piedmont Scouts from Troops 11, 1, and 4 traveled to the U.S. Virgin Islands Sea Base for a 7-day snorkeling and sailing trip. Accompanying them were five troop parents. The trip, originally planned for 2020, was delayed because of COVID- 19. On this trip, the group followed COVID safety protocols, including testing negative for COVID before traveling, wearing masks in all public areas, and frequent hand washing. When the Scouts arrived, they split into two predetermined crews, one travelling on the 62- foot Moondance, a ketch rig sailboat with a mainsail, a jib, and a mizzenmast. and the other group on the Galateia, a 45-foot sloop with a mainsail and a jib. School is out and the weather is good, so the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group decided it was a good time to visit Beach School and the Linda Playfield next to it. Two dozen walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra on a lovely morning, July 14, to take a long walk. On hand were: Dave DeRoche, Fia Hsu, Jim Kuo, Sherry Jacobs, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 friend Chili, Adrienne Hamlin, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Quincy Dong, Melba Yee, Alan Goldhammer, Nancy Olsen, Larry Olsen, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Phil Witte, Priscilla Wanerus, Swee Ling Chen, Helen Dong, Albert Chen, Stella Houston, Haybert Houston, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome first-time walker Carol Lyons. A long line of walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue, went on Bonita and caused a minor traffic delay while crossing Oakland Avenue due to the size of the group. Some walkers said they hadn’t recently walked on Bonita and admired the homes and yards. The group paused at Latham Street, where they were joined for the first time by Rebekah Wildman and Michael Denning. It was an ideal time for one of the group’s favorite trivia questions: What is the only street in Piedmont? The answer is Latham Street. All other streets are named Avenue, Drive, Road, Way or Boulevard. They continued on Oakland Avenue to an entry to Linda Playfield on Howard Avenue, but found the gate locked with a chain and a sign saying the field was closed for summer Rec, Department youth activities. On the field were a swarm of young people enjoying themselves. While there they talked about its history, the townhomes recently built replacing a former PG&E substation, as well as the City’s plans for future development of the space. The walkers went up Howard to Lake Avenue and a half block to the entrance of Beach School where they talked about the school’s history and took a group photo. The history of Beach School starts with the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. Thousands of people fled the city, and many made their new homes in the East Bay. In fact, Piedmont grew ten times over the next year and was incorporated in September 1907. The city’s leaders decided to build two schools to serve the growing community. Piedmont’s first school (Havens) opened in 1911 and was originally named the Bonita Avenue School. It was later renamed Frank C. Havens School after the land donor. It quickly filled to capacity and the Lake Avenue School was built in 1913 to meet the demand for more classrooms. Four teachers taught 100 students in six grades. In 1918 the school was renamed the Egbert W. Beach School in honor of Egbert William Beach, the first Piedmont resident to give his life in World War I. Beach School’s original building was condemned as a fire and earthquake danger in 1933. It was torn down in 1934 and replaced by two separate WPA projects. The school’s main wing was built in 1936 and the auditorium and classroom wing was added in 1940. The school enjoyed the long-tenured guidance of Piedmonter Nancy McHugh, who served as principal from 1979 to 2007. Later, as part of a set of citywide school seismic upgrades, Beach hosted part of Havens School’s student body for the 2009-10 school year while aa new Havens School was being built. The following year, Wildwood School students also shared the Beach campus when their school was being reconstructed. articles.text: Dear Jim: We have an older home and are looking to carve out more space. With our growing family, an older daughter now back home, and the possibility of my mom moving in with us, we either need to add on or move. We love our home, community, and neighbors, and would prefer to stay put. What are our options? This is a common question in my business. Fortunately, most homeowners have options for gaining additional space and making their homes operate more efficiently in the process. Up or down, in or out The most obvious question is, “where do we add additional space?” If you add going up you typically gain more light, a view, and warmer rooms. Rear additions are more straightforward projects if you have yard space. One potential downside to additions is running into design review and neighbor input. If you add a basement, it is typically cooler, quieter, feels more separate, and is easier to permit. Basement projects involve major structural and foundation work, and usually require replacement of the home’s utilities. Since the infrastructure is often in need of replacement anyway in older homes, redesigning the lower level can allow for adding more efficient systems which use less space. Occasionally your home’s existing floor plan can be modified as the simplest option. What is the most cost-effective? Basement jobs and second (or third) floor additions are the most expensive projects but can literally double the size of your home. They can dramatically increase your home’s value and can be a game changer if you need a lot of space. Rear additions are usually more cost effective, but you need enough lot size to meet code requirements. If you have existing spaces that can be reconfigured, interior changes are usually the least expensive. Examples are adding a half bath to a closet or splitting up a large room to add an office. We have remodeled homes where we added a bedroom and a bathroom to the current space just by moving a few walls and doors around. Eliminating a second-floor unused deck allows space for a new addition. Dig deep! Upgrading and moving furnaces or water heaters out of basements to crawlspaces can create more useable floorspace. There are many options to explore depending on your budget, the creativity of your design team, and your current floor plan. Your next step would be to start researching contractors in your area who can assist you to dig out your home’s hidden treasures to create more space! City Council were unified in their decision to reject an appeal, but it appears that the city is swimming uphill in the flow of public opinion. Piedmont has been fully built out for nearly 50 years. To meet the daunting task of creating over 500 new and affordable housing units, city council created a Housing Advisory Committee, whose members will review and provide feedback on the development and conduct of all tasks under this scope of work. Potentially adding to Piedmont’s burden, if an appeal of a jurisdiction is successful, ABAG must redistribute the units to other local governments within the region to satisfy the total 441,176 units assigned to the nine counties and 101 cities within the Bay Area. For example, Clayton – with approximately the same population as Piedmont – is requesting to decrease its draft RHNA allocation by 285 units. If Clayton succeeds in its appeal, those units will be allocated to a different jurisdiction, possibly Piedmont. “Clayton is a largely built-out community, with minimum land available for urban development,” said Clayton City Manager Reina Schwartz. “The 6th RHNA cycle number of 570 units is nearly 400% more [than the last cycle] and does not reflect the limited land available for development in the city.” Piedmont has been told by the state to create 587 new housing units, a 979% increase. The city is moving forward optimistically, though, with public outreach efforts via a website (PiedmontIsHome.org) and ongoing housing advisory meetings. On Friday, July 23, a Piedmont family installed a 350-square foot Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) on their property, using a crane to lift the granny-flat into place [see story on Front page]. As the next RHNA cycle approaches, the city and its residents will have to continue to find creative ways to produce more units within geographical constraints in order to meet that state mandate. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department will bring back its popular Movies in the Park summer series this Friday, July 30, with a screening in Piedmont Park of Sing, a 2016 animated movie perfect for entire family. All movies are at dusk and are free. Bring a blanket, low profile lawn chairs and some popcorn while enjoying a film on the lawn under the stars. In this animated 2016 film, Buster Moon the Koala takes one final chance to restore his once majestic theater to its former glory by producing the world’s greatest singing competition. Five contestants emerge in this knee slapping comedy produced by Illumination: a mouse, a timid elephant, a pig, a gorilla and a punk-rock porcupine. Get in on the fun of this popular children’s movie before the anticipated sequel Sing 2 comes out in December.
